question: What changes when the same strain is told a third time?
intro: A storyteller’s strain in D major is told, then told again, and returns between two short slurred interludes. Listen for how Schumann changes the telling by changing only the dynamic.

sections.label: A · the story told twice
sections.mNote: two eight-bar tellings, written out in full

cues.title: A tune that begins on the upbeat
cues.text: Three beats to the bar in D major, marked mf. The tune starts on an upbeat and bounces over detached left-hand chords, with the pedal marked from the first bar. Each telling ends in a rising run to an accented chord.
cues.evidence: First edition pp. 4–5 (IMSLP #03060): D major, 3/4, mf, upbeat start, pedal marked, run to an accented chord at the end of each eight-bar group. The report reads D major (r = 0.75) with F♯ A G among the strongest pitch classes at 0:00 and a level near −7 dB at 0:05.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Told twice, written out
cues.text: Bars 9–16 repeat bars 1–8, but the repeat is written out in full, not marked with a sign. Each telling lasts about eighteen seconds here, so the second begins near 0:18.
cues.evidence: The form analysis matches 0:02–0:15 with 0:19–0:32 (lag 17 s, mean similarity 0.98, the closest match in this piece). The score prints bars 1–8 and 9–16 as two identical groups of notes.

cues.title: Four bars under one slur
cues.text: After the second telling the music drops to piano and sings four bars under a single long slur. The run and the accents of the story give way to a smoother line, and the bass settles on G.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.96 at 0:36 and 0.96 at 0:46, with the bass on G and a level fall to −13.8 dB at 0:40. Score p. 4 (last system): p, one slur over four bars.

cues.title: Titles sent with a warning
cues.text: Schumann sent Clara a list of titles that includes “Curiose Geschichte”, and told her the pieces would please her but that she must “forget herself as a virtuoso”. His phrase is “als Virtuosin vergeßen”; Clara was then a celebrated pianist in Vienna.
cues.evidence: Letter begun 17 March 1838, quoted in the Zwickau catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen, item 3, with the title list; the Henle Urtext review at schumann-portal.de/3213.html dates the letter 19 March. Clara’s Vienna recitals: December 1837 to April 1838 (Nancy Reich, Clara Schumann).

cues.title: A ritardando before the last telling
cues.text: At the end of the third telling the score asks for a ritardando. In the recording the level dips near 1:00, then the slurred bars come back briefly before the story is told for the last time.
cues.evidence: Report: −19.0 dB at 1:00 (the second-quietest window of the piece), novelty 0.80 at 0:58 and 0.81 at 1:04. Score p. 5: ritard. at the end of the third telling.

cues.title: The last telling slows to a close
cues.text: The final telling is marked mf and ends with a ritardando into the closing bar. The sound has faded almost completely by about 1:35.
cues.evidence: Form analysis: 0:41–1:01 matches 1:12–1:32 (mean 0.95); report novelty 1.00 at 1:18, level −35.2 dB at 1:35. Score p. 5 (last system): mf, ritard., final bar.

transitions.title: The run gives way to a long slur
transitions.how: Each telling ends with a rising run to an accented chord. After the second, the music drops to p and the detached chords of the story give way to four bars under one slur. The metre is still three beats to the bar; the change is of touch and dynamic, and the bass moves away from D towards G.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.96 at 0:36, level −13.8 dB at 0:40, bass on G. The score (p. 4, last system) puts p and a four-bar slur after the second run.

transitions.title: The upbeat brings the story back
transitions.how: The slurred bars end and the upbeat figure of the opening returns, now marked p where the first telling was mf. The tune is the same; the dynamic alone changes the meaning, so the story sounds confided rather than announced.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.96 at 0:46 and loud windows at 0:45–0:50. The form analysis matches 0:41–1:01 with 1:12–1:32. Score p. 5, first system: p over the returning strain.

transitions.title: A ritardando hands over to the slur
transitions.how: The third telling ends with a marked ritard. on its run, so the music has almost stopped when the four slurred bars enter under p. The same plan as before (run, slowing, smooth line) is repeated with the slowing now written into the score.
transitions.evidence: Report: level −19.0 dB at 1:00, novelty 0.80 at 0:58 and 0.81 at 1:04. Score p. 5: ritard. at the end of the third telling, then the slurred bars.

transitions.title: The upbeat returns for the last time
transitions.how: The upbeat figure returns once more, marked mf as at the start. This telling is the one that ends with a ritardando and the final bar, where the earlier tellings led on to the slurred bars.
transitions.evidence: Form analysis: 0:41–1:01 matches 1:12–1:32, so the last telling begins near 1:12; report novelty 1.00 at 1:18. Score p. 5, last system: mf and ritard. to the final bar.

composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
